articles.text: Everyone is invited to attend our annual free Christmas Concert presented by First Church of Christ, Scientist, in Oakland’s Montclair district. The 90-minute concert will take place at 3 p.m. on December 21, 2025, at the church, located at 1880 Mountain Blvd, Oakland. This year’s theme is from the book of Isaiah, “The government shall be upon his shoulder,” (Isaiah 9:6), and will feature congregational caroling. Christmas favorites and new arrangements will be performed by talented Bay Area musicians: soprano Katy Stephan, mezzo-soprano Tracy Hinman, tenor Michael Belle, baritone Steve Rogino, operachi vocalist Juanita Ulloa performing songs in Spanish, guitarist Derek Brooker, pianist/organist Michael Moran, and Virginia Morgan on viola. Admission is free. Wheelchair accessible with our new ADA ramp and restrooms. Parking is available across the street from the church at Montclair Elementary School. articles.text: Nacho is a friendly, handsome cat with a big appreciation for the good things in life: a warm bed, a full bowl, and people who love him. He’s confident, affectionate, and very much a “shadow cat” who enjoys being near his people— greeting you with cheerful meows, chatting back when you talk to him, and sometimes even giving your arm or leg a little groom to show his affection. Nacho loves attention and play, especially interactive wand toys that let him stalk and pounce like a pro. He plays in enthusiastic bursts, and also enjoys quiet companionship, sometimes sleeping near his guardian at night. While he’s not a lap cat, he does love cuddles and being picked up. He can get a bit overstimulated when excited about food, petting, or play, so he’ll do best with a cat-savvy adopter who can read his cues and help him channel that enthusiasm in Adopt Nacho through Cat Town. positive ways. Nacho does have ongoing medical needs, including asthma and food allergies, which are currently well managed with a special diet and a daily inhaler—something he’s learned to accept with treats and patience. He’s seeking an adopter with some experience, a calm home with teens, and possibly another cat companion. Nacho is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV and FIV. Since 1993, the WHOF has honored women whose leadership, innovation, and service have strengthened Alameda County’s diverse communities. “For more than three decades, the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame has celebrated the achievements of remarkable women who are shaping our communities for the better,” said Susan S. Muranishi, Alameda County Administrator and Co-Chair of the Women’s Hall of Fame. “We invite residents to help us honor these changemakers by nominating women who exemplify leadership, compassion, and service.” Through the Mary V. King/ Wilma Chan Youth Scholarship Fund, WHOF will also award up to six $5,000 scholarships to outstanding high school seniors who demonstrate academic excellence, community involvement, leadership, and perseverance in overcoming challenges. Up to twelve inductees and six youth scholarship recipients will be honored at the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame Luncheon and Awards Ceremony. Proceeds from the event and related activities help fund programs that support women and families across Alameda County. Community members are invited to nominate inspiring women in the following categories: Business & Professions, Culture & Art, Community Service, Education, Emerging Leaders, Environmental, Health, Justice, Non-Traditional, Philanthropy, Science/Technology/Engineering, and Sports & Athletics. For nomination and scholarship details, visit www.acgov. org/whof

articles.text: Piedmont voters appear poised to renew the Measure G parcel tax, according to results presented at the Dec. 10 school board meeting. Consultant Dr. Tim McLarney of True North reported that a recent survey showed strong support for continuing the tax, which provides about $12 million a year for local schools, roughly 20 percent of the district’s budget. Based on the findings, the district plans to place the Measure G renewal on the June ballot. The survey reached 342 likely voters by phone, email and text. An initial ballot test projected 84% support, well above the twothirds threshold required for passage. Of those surveyed, 51.5% said they would “definitely” vote yes, while 32.8% said they would “probably” vote yes. “I can say that in my career I struggle to think of examples, other than in Piedmont, where we have had initial ballot tests in the 80s,” McLarney said. He joined the meeting remotely, along with district consultant Larry Tramatola, who was present in person. At its next meeting on January 7, the board plans to adopt a resolution formally placing the measure on the June ballot. Board members also discussed adding language to “evergreen” the tax, allowing it to continue without a set expiration date, with an annual 3% increase to keep pace with inflation. “Could that resolution include language to keep this Measure G parcel tax at the same base rate structure, an annual increase for inflation, probably 3 percent, and language to evergreen this parcel tax?” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn asked. All five board members supported including that language. “The fact it’s an evergreen proposal is a huge relief, because our district can’t function without that. That’s wonderful,” said APT President Elise Marks. Board members, students and teachers expressed appreciation for the community’s ongoing support of local schools. Following the January 7 resolution, the district plans to begin its campaign for the June election, with Ted Kinch and Rebecca Pelle serving as campaign co-chairs.
articles.title: Parcel Tax survey says: Yes!

articles.text: During the December 10 Piedmont School Board meeting Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) President Elise Marks brought up a recent negotiation session with the district that she deemed unsuccessful and disheartening. District negotiation sessions between labor groups, like the teachers and CSEA workers, are held in closed session. Currently, working conditions, but not salaries, are up for discussion. “We came out of this round feeling that district leadership was not willing to move meaningfully on anything,” said Marks. Marks reported that teachers filled out surveys, necessary so the school can obtain its WACS accreditation and recertification, of how well current district structures are supporting student success and student well-being. Marks said the scores were not good. At the end of her statement, with union members in mass behind her, Marks concluded that the Association of Piedmont Teacher will not threaten a strike, they will take their offers off the table, and will prepare for negotiations in the spring. “APT is choosing not to go to impasse. We will agree to mutually withdraw all proposals on both sides, and focus on a return to the bargaining table as early as possible in the spring as our entire contract is open again,” said Marks. An overarching concern was raised that teachers are not having their voices heard. “In the last few years we have experienced a profound shift: teachers are being left out of major conversations. We learn about many decisions only as they are announced to the public, not before,” said Marks. In response to the Mark’s quote immediately above, School Board President Ruchi Medhekar responded to the Post with “We respectfully disagree with this characterization. We’ve significantly expanded teacher voice in decision-making.” Medhekar and the board pointed to five examples of teacher involvement including engagement via district-level meetings, and programs initiated by the district teachers like the new 6th and 7th grade language programs and the Fishtank curriculum for elementary language arts. “We reversed course on sophomore honors English and history based directly on teacher and community feedback,” Medhekar said. President Medhekar added that the board now shares all policy changes with labor partners at least ten days before Board discussion to ensure meaningful input. In their current round of negotiations teachers were asking for hard caps to class sizes to formally prohibit enormous classes. “Our contract language is very soft on class size,” said Marks. Sometimes the text of their contract says “every effort will be made” by the district. APT wants clear and unambiguous contract language on this to prevent teachers from being saddled with up to 37 students. The district sees the progress of their negotiations in a significantly different light. “Although we did not reach formal agreement on any items, we identified common ground, including our mutual desire to reopen negotiations early in the spring and our shared commitment to ensuring balanced and manageable class sizes across all grades, which we look forward to revisiting after we return from winter break,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn in an email to the Post. “Teachers are with students, boots on the ground, all day long, making school happen. We see things that administrators and parents just don’t have the opportunity to see,” said Marks. What voices will be heard and at what volume remains to be seen, but both sides have work to be done to repair their relationships. Maybe the holiday spirit and a little break can help return hope.
articles.title: Teachers ask for their voices to be heard

articles.text: The instructional calendar for the 2026-27 school year proffered by Piedmont teachers was approved by the school district via the consent calendar at the December 10 school board meeting. Next year’s school schedule, which mirrors this year’s, was approved, but the board chose not to approve it for two years, as has been custom. The district did not approve the calendar for its second year because the schedule the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) offered did not reflect any changes the district wanted based on a parent survey. “The APT contract provides language that describes what teachers will do, including presenting calendars for two years to the Board. That contract language was met at the November Board meeting. However, the Board decided to approve only one year, which occurred at the December Board meeting,” explains Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. APT did not want to shorten the first semester to achieve a midweek start to the first week or a later first day of school. The current schedule, which will be in effect for next year, starts the school year on a Monday, and keeps first semester finals before Winter Break.
articles.title: Next year’s school instructional calendar approved

Exploration of the Ice Giants and Beyond The harsh conditions of Uranus and Neptune, combined with their distance from Earth, have made exploration challenging. To date, NASA’s Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited both planets, flying by Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. After cresting the top of the Geneva Spur ridge, Bill Baringer traverses the long granite slate before Camp Four at 26,300.’ The narrow paths on Summit Ridge have fixed rope lines installed by Sherpas every May. Each line is held by ice screws, at times holding thousands of pounds of climbers. survive Everest,” explained Baringer. On May 5, 2019 they received the green light for their third rotation up the mountain. They stayed at Camp One for a night, Camp Two for a night, then used their ascenders to clip onto the fixed lines for the ascent up the steep ice wall to “touch” Camp Three and descend the same day. When coming back down from Camp Three a cluster of ice and rock chunks cascaded down from above. A rock projectile hit the leg of climbing guide Pemba and tore through his pants and socks, gashing a hole in his leg. Baringer helped Pemba bandage his leg, offered his ski poles and helped him down to camp. Pemba was flown down the mountain by helicopter to get stitched back up. Three days later Pemba flew back up to help the team summit Everest. Another high wind weather delay turned Everest Base Camp into a waiting room. Many climbing teams were held up there, so nearly everyone eyed May 21 as the window of opportunity to reach the top. “No one knew if there was going to be another window after that, and the season closed on May 30. We weren’t going to wait for the 28,” said Baringer. Finally, they got the call to start the final rotation on May 17. The now familiar, 2:00 a.m. alarm clock commenced the move to Camp One at 19,500’ for a one-night stay. Here the Sherpas served Baringer spicy ramen soup, also known as “Sherpa Down Jacket.” The trip up to Camp Two at 21,500’ took three hours on May 18. The next day took them up to Camp Three at 23,500’, their first overnight at this height. Oxygen bottles were brought out to be used for the rest of the trip. May 20 marked new territory for Baringer on the way up to Camp Four at 26,300’. The route featured the infamous “Yellow Band” section of rock to be managed with crampons designed for snow. Baringer recalled the uneasy memory of balancing on the tips of his crampons. “Front-pointing on granite just seemed wrong,” he recalled. After Yellow Band, Baringer faced the first bad traffic jam on a steep rocky segment called “Geneva Spur.” In trying to get past a boulder on the slope Baringer pulled on two separate fixed lines. When one broke, he swayed and fell, but his ascender on the other rope held fast – another close call. After Geneva Spur, the group sighted the rocky Camp Four, the area known as the “Death Zone” where the ambient oxygen is 30 percent of the value at sea level. Baringer describes the camp five miles above sea level. “It was a disaster. All the lower camps were pristine, super clean. I’m sure they did some cleaning there, but you were still left with canisters, tent poles, and shrapnel everywhere. It looked like a bomb went off,” he said. The guides planned for a few hours of rest before attempting the summit that night. But the winds were howling, so an extra day was spent at Camp Four. The next day Baringer’s guides decided they were not going to start at the usual 10 p.m., but at 5:30 p.m. to climb all night and summit before sunrise on Wednesday, May 22. They started early because of the anticipated crowds. Photos that became famous throughout the world showed a long, congested queue to summit. “It wasn’t because there were so many mountaineers on the mountain itself. It’s that they were all attempting their summit bids on the same day,” explained Baringer. Climbing Everest in the dark turned out to be very prudent. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team got its season started in a big way, winning its own Paris Twins Classic for the first time since the 2022. The Highlanders opened with a 91-35 win over Oakland High on Thursday, December 11, beat Vanden in the semifinals 85-43 the following day, and won 64-50 over Cardinal Newman on Saturday, December 13. Their win over the Cardinals was a match of two top-10 Bay Area teams. Before the game, Cal-Hi Sports had Cardinal Newman ranked No. 4 in its top-10 list and Piedmont as No. 5. Just three games into the season, beating Cardinal Newman was important to help build Piedmont’s candidacy for a North Coast Section Open Division bid at the end of the regular season. articles.text: Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored the game-winning goal against Marin Academy Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team captured its first win of the season with a 1-nil victory over Marin Academy in San Rafael on Saturday, December 13. The result brings PHS’ record to 1-1-2 (W-T-L) through its first four games. Piedmont’s goal came from Miranda Liu in the 54th minute when she scored on a penalty kick. The foul came after a handball by a Marin Academy player in the penalty area. Piedmont goalkeeper Rachel Young also had one of the most critical plays in the game in the first half to preserve a 0-0 tie through the first 40 minutes. The Highlanders were penalized for a back pass in their own box in the 22nd minute, leading to an awkward in-direct free kick near the penalty spot. Marin Academy played a low shot through the defense, but Young quickly blocked the shot with her foot. Piedmont has two matches left before the New Year. They are set to host Oakland Tech today, December 17, and will play neighboring Head-Royce in Oakland on Friday, December 19. Match Recap Piedmont had the game’s first shot attempt in the fifth minute, when Ayla Blanford sent a shot wide of the net. Liu also had a shot trail wide in the 10th minute. PHS’ next chance came in the 20th minute, when a long pass from a corner fell to Blanford, who tried to chip a shot to the far post. However, her shot was cleared away. Marin Academy had a critical scoring chance in the 22nd when Piedmont was penalized for a back pass in its own box. That’s what led to Young making her instinctive kick save to keep the game deadlocked at 0-0. The second half started with back-and-forth action without either side having overtly dangerous chances. Marin Academy had a shot blocked by Darcy McKee in the 41st minute, then had a shot trail wide two minutes later. In the 53rd minute, Piedmont was awarded its penalty kick when a Marin Academy defender failed to clear a ball, kicking it high into the sky instead of out her own box. Another Wildcat’s defender missed on a header clearance, leading to the ball back spinning off the turf and into her hand. Liu stepped to the spot, sending her shot to the left of the keeper to give PHS a 1-nil lead. That was the only shot Piedmont needed from then on. Marin Academy had a slow shot handled by Young in the 55th, then had a long shot from about 30 yards easily saved by Young. Young came up with another critical save in the 68th minute at the end of a corner. The Wildcats sent a high looping cross, leading to a header attempt that skipped off the ground and toward net. Young was ranging to her right, and reached back to her left to get a hand on the shot, pouncing on it to regain possession. Both teams traded possession for the remaining 12 minutes of regulation. articles.text: With basketball being the only overlapping winter sport between high school and college, we take a look at former basketball stars still active in college: Natalia Martinez at San Diego State, A.J. Harris at Emory University, and Eva Levingston at Robert Morris University. NATALIA MARTINEZ San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, in currently in her sophomore season at San Diego State and is close to being the Aztecs’ leading scorer. She was the Post’s only back-to-back Athlete of the Year award winner (2023 and 2024). This year, San Diego State is 6-3 through a 29-game regular season schedule. Martinez is second on the team in scoring and minutes with 113 points and 239 minutes. She’s currently hitting 34 percent of her 3-pointers. She scored a season-high of 24 points on November 24 against Penn State, and this week was named the Mountain West Conference Player of the Week. Martinez was impressive as a freshman last season, making the MWC All-Freshman team. They won the conference title as the No. 4 seed and earned the No. 14 ranking in the NCAA’s March Madness tournament. The Aztecs went up against No. 2 LSU, which made it to the Elite Eight. Martinez was in the starting five, playing 27 minutes for seven points, and had one rebound and one assist. She set a MWC record in an 85-66 win over Utah State, where she became the first player to ever sink six 3-pointers in a conference game. In her record-setting performance, Martinez finished with 22 points, converting 7/8 from the field and 6/7 for 3-pointers. She hit one of her 3-pointers from around seven feet behind the 3-point line. Photo courtesy of San Diego State Natalia Martinez, PHS Class of 2024, is a sophomore at San Diego State and is challenging to lead the team in scoring. Harris appeared in all 29 games for 825 minutes, scoring 336 points by shooting 45 percent from the field and 33 percent from 3-pointers, to go along with 149 rebounds, 43 assists, 42 steals and seven blocks. Harris notched a career-high of 28 points in a 77-71 win over Union College. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s All-Time leading scorer with 1,570 points after playing in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID-19. We named Harris the Posts’ 2023 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year. team in Pittsburgh after playing the first two years of her collegiate career at Cal State Fullerton. articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”
articles.title: ’Twas the Night Before Christmas

articles.text: Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers in 1818, the answer was an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ had broken with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices – equally straightforward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later, the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years, it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades, uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a courtroom trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818, they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we can still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We can create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fourth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: pear tree. a partridge in a pear tree. partridge in a pear tree.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 17, 2025 17 The 12 Days of Christmas Background of the Song The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. articles.text: Center Repertory Company, in partnership with AXIS Dance Company, premiered a new adaptation of Charles Dickens’ holiday classic “A Christmas Carol,” bringing together an award-winning creative team for what the company calls its most ambitious seasonal production to date. The all-new staging reimagines the familiar story through the eyes of young Tim Cratchit, who makes a wish on a candle that summons a series of ghostly visitors to the bedside of the famously miserly Ebenezer Scrooge. The adaptation is written by playwright Harrison David Rivers, whose retelling emphasizes compassion and responsibility toward society’s most vulnerable. While remaining faithful to Dickens’ original narrative, the production frames the story as a contemporary meditation on empathy, generosity and the human cost of valuing profit over people. The production is described as Center REP’s grandest interpretation of the Dickens classic and marks a premiere for the company. Center REP is the resident professional theater company of the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek. Led by Artistic Director Matt M. Morrow and Managing Director Carolyn Jackson, the company was founded in 1968 and is among the oldest professional theaters in the Bay Area. “Our West Coast premiere of this new holiday tradition is the cornerstone of the Lesher Center’s 35th Anniversary. This milestone for our beloved home is all about shaping the future, and Harrison’s adaptation is nothing if not forward facing,” said Center Rep Artistic Director Matt Murrow. Director Jared Mezzocchi, who previously introduced Center REP’s “FROGGY,” leads the production. Mezzocchi employs an immersive digital design to bring Victorian London and its supernatural netherworld vividly to life, blending traditional storytelling with modern theatrical technology. A Christmas Carol is showing onstage this Thursday through Sunday. Runtime is approximately two hours including one 15-minute intermission. Lesher Center for the Arts is located at 1601 Civic Drive in Walnut Creek, California, in downtown Walnut Creek’s arts district. Visit https://www.centerrep.org/whats-on/25-26-season/a-christmascarol to purchase tickets or call the box office at (925) 943-7469. Photo by Kevin Berne Brayden K. Sinkay as “Tim”, and Danny J. Gomez as “Man” in Center REP’s A Christmas Carol.

articles.text: On December 9, 1965, nearly half of U.S. TV sets were tuned to one unlikely show: “A Charlie Brown Christmas.” With its jazz score by Vince Guaraldi and using amateur voice actors, it was predicted to be a flop. Instead, it has become a beloved annual tradition. The show, based on Charles Schulz’s Peanuts cartoon series, was premiered that day by a major TV network, and subsequently became available everywhere to watch around the holidays. Piedmont Center for the Arts this year celebrates the program’s 60th anniversary with a live concert version of “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” with Vince Guaraldi’s classic score played by the jazz trio of Larry Dunlap, piano, Akira Tana, drums, and Ken Miller on bass – plus live narration by the performers. Dress your family in Peanuts-inspired costumes and bring them to a show that will spark nostalgia for you, delight your children and bring holiday spirit to everyone. Two performances back to back on the Sunday before Christmas, December 21. Performance times are 12 noon and 1:30 p.m. Advance tickets are highly recommended as space is limited. Buy tickets at https://www.brownpapertickets.com/e/6756087.

articles.text: Berkeley City Ballet, the East Bay’s premiere training school for classical ballet, presents its 51st annual Nutcracker at the Alan Harvey Theater on the Piedmont High School campus on Saturday, December 20. Following a sold out run of its debut at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School last year, the ballet company is returning to Piedmont to showcase the holiday classic, featuring dancers from the company’s pre-professional program as well as professional guests artists from ballet companies including Boulder Ballet and Ballet Memphis. Berkeley City Ballet, founded in 1974, presents one of the East Bay’s few traditional, full-length productions of the Nutcracker, complete with classic characters Clara and the Nutcracker Prince, with traditional settings like the enchanting Land of the Sweets. Two performances are held at 1:00 p.m. and 5:00 p.m. General admission tickets are $35. Purchase tickets at https://berkeleycityballet.org/nutcracker/.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet Tickets to Oakland Ballet’s popular holiday performance The Nutcracker are limited. Oakland Ballet will present its production of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker this weekend, December 20 and 21, at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Limited tickets are available for purchase online. Oakland Ballet dancers bring Artistic Director Lustig’s classic holiday ensemble to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The production features more than 40 dancers aged 7 to 17, in the roles of snowballs, mice, soldiers and candies, performing alongside Oakland Ballet dancers. The Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will deliver Tchaikovsky’s magnificent score, marking the 54th year that Oakland Ballet has presented a production of The Nutcracker in the East Bay. This year’s production coincides with Oakland Ballet’s 60th anniversary. Running time is approximately two hours including intermission, and doors open one hour before showtime. Both performances begin at 1 p.m. Performances are family-friendly and all ages require a ticket. Guests may add on a ticket for the “Sweet Dreams Party” on December 20, where ticket-holders of all ages will meet the cast and characters of The Nutcracker, pose for photographs, collect autographs, and enjoy treats and refreshments. Tickets are available online now. To purchase tickets, visit https://oaklandballet.org/ or call the Paramount box office number 510-465-6400.

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet presents a special matinee performance of Nutcracker geared toward neurodivergent audience members on Sunday, December 28. The company introduced its first-ever sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on December 21, 2022. The event is presented in collaboration with Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area. Special accommodations have been made to the Nutcracker for the performance that are friendly to those who experience sensory processing disorders, autism, post traumatic stress disorder, and all neurodiverse audiences. It takes place in a relaxed and “shushfree” setting and is appropriate for all ages, and designated quiet areas will be available for guests. “As a musician, and parent of an autistic son, I’m especially sensitive to how much music and dance can touch the hearts of people with autism and special needs,” Stephen Prutsman, President of Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area, said in 2022. “The holiday season can be stressful and isolating for autism and special needs families, so for a world-class company like San Francisco Ballet to open its doors and welcome our community is a landmark for the entire ballet world, and a tremendous gift for us.” This family-friendly performance also serves as an opportunity for first-time balletgoers and young children to experience ballet in a more informal setting. This special version of Nutcracker is open to all audience members; but because it is adapted specifically to accommodate individuals with sensory sensitivities, guests are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the adjustments of the Sensory Friendly Performance. The performance begins at 11 a.m. Visit www.sfballet.org to purchase tickets and to learn more about sensory friendly performances. The ballet company partners with the Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area to deliver a sensory-friendly performance of Nutcracker appropriate for all ages.

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California is hosting an afternoon of live performances and celebrating the Persian holiday of Yalda this Sunday, December 21. The event coincides with the Winter Solstice and features performances by internationally-acclaimed Iranian Bay Areabased singers Mahsa Vahdat and Marjan Vahdat, accompanied by musician and writer Atabak Elyasi. Yalda, also known as Shab-e Yalda, is an ancient Persian holiday marking the winter solstice, the longest night of the year. Observed on the evening of December 21, the celebration has roots stretching back more than 2,000 years to pre-Islamic Iran, where it symbolized the triumph of light over darkness and the promise of longer days ahead. Families and friends traditionally gather after sunset and remain together until midnight or later, sharing food, poetry and conversation. Seasonal fruits such as pomegranates and watermelon are staples of the night, their red color representing life and renewal. Reading from the works of the 14th-century poet Hafez is a common custom, with verses interpreted as reflections on the year ahead. Yalda is celebrated by Iranians of all backgrounds, as well as Persian-speaking communities in countries including Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and among the Iranian diaspora worldwide. pages.text: Wednesday, December 17, 2025 21 Features Pawsitive Touch: Essential Handling Exercises for Your New Puppy By Sierra Berrick Bringing home a new puppy can be overwhelming, and prioritizing trust and respect is key. Teaching your puppy to accept handling and restraint is crucial for their safety and is even more important than obedience or socialization. It is essential to teach your puppy to respect your right to examine them and restrain them, as this could save their life in an emergency. The following handling exercises will help strengthen your bond and increase your puppy’s comfort with handling and restraint. Cradling: Hold your puppy like a baby, cupping one hand around their chest and under their chin so they do not have access to your hand with their mouth. Give the command “settle” and examine them closely, using your other hand to spread out their toes, check inside their ears or mouth, and rub their belly. If they struggle or vocalize, hug them firmly and give a verbal negative marker (“uh uh”) before repeating the “settle” command. Be sure to release puppies only when they are calm. Side Exam and Flipping Over: Lay your puppy on their side and place your arm along their body to keep their head and shoulders down. Continue the body examination, using your A collie puppy modeling the cradling exercise during a puppy class forearm to keep them in place if needed. When calm, grab the puppy’s front legs in one hand and rear legs in the other, then flip them over to their other side gently but swiftly. Repeat the exam. Stand, Sit, Down: Take one hand under their chin and one hand under their belly to place them in a standing position. Then, scoop under their rear legs to sit them down (don’t push down on their hips!), and finally, take their front legs and place them in a down position. Troubleshooting: If your puppy bites, firmly wrap your hand around their muzzle and say “no bite!” Repeat if necessary as they may think this a game at first. Also, be prepared for the occasional temper tantrum when your puppy is still getting used to extensive handling. They may vocalize excessively or attempt to squirm. Respond by giving a verbal negative marker and reinforce the “settle“ command by holding your puppy more firmly until they relax. It is essential to only release puppies from handling when they are calm. These exercises (originally from Mike Wombacher’s Puppy One course), will help build a strong bond and prepare your puppy for life’s challenges. Large, wall-mounted displays allow dispatchers to monitor public safety cameras and automated license plate readers. After thanking Chief Shavies and Gonzales for the tour, the group continued their weekly walk through nearby neighborhoods. They first headed down Magnolia Avenue for another look at the new Community Pool, which remains closed and is now expected to open in the spring due to equipment delays. From there, the walkers visited several “one-block wonder” streets known for their charm and history. On Carmel Avenue, they revisited landscaping and stonework highlighted during a 2023 walk by architect, urban designer, and Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams, who died last year after a stroke. The walk continued up Blair Avenue to Dracena Avenue and along Park Way, where recent cold, wet weather had produced a striking bloom of large mushrooms. The group’s final stop was Waldo Avenue, tied to Piedmont’s early history as the former rear boundary of Walter Blair’s 19th-century home. articles.text: If old foundation needs replacement A significant number of older homes are experiencing settlement problems, cracking, sloping floors, drainage issues and other infrastructure concerns related to 100-year-old foundations that may need replacement. A common question from homeowners facing this work is whether this is the right time to add more space in the basement. Many people consider expanding their homes to accommodate additional family members, create a second unit, or add a bedroom, workshop, office, utility or media room, storage space, or some combination of these uses. The pros of a new basement renovation If significant foundation work is already planned, this may be the only practical opportunity to add usable space beneath your home. A new foundation design is typically more substantial than the original and can accommodate increased ceiling heights. Because basement work requires comprehensive drainage solutions and addresses underlying structural issues, combining the projects can allow you to tackle multiple problems at once. Basement jobs are big projects These projects begin with excavating more soil than most homeowners anticipate. From there, contractors build tall retaining foundation walls with extensive rebar, install wholehouse drainage systems, pour new reinforced concrete floors, and add new walls, beams and seismic upgrades. This phase typically takes about three months. The remodel itself is a larger undertaking, often lasting six months. It frequently requires reworking plumbing, electrical and mechanical systems that are outdated or need to be relocated. Does this make sense to do These jobs are far more expensive than many people expect, so the decision often comes down to budget and necessity. Homeowners can expect to spend about $600 per square foot or more for the project from start to finish, with roughly half of the cost going toward the dig-out and half toward the remodel. One common cost-saving strategy, if time allows, is to divide the work into two phases. Phase one completes the digout and prepares the space for remodeling. Phase two proceeds later, as budget and timing permit, sometimes with homeowners hiring carpenters and individual trades rather than a general contractor for the entire scope. Adding habitable space increases a home’s square footage and can raise its value, often exceeding the cost of the work itself. Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. Jim is a longtime Piedmont resident and has been doing foundation replacement, drainage work, structural repair and basement dig outs in your neighborhood since 1983. articles.text: Robert Hendrickson of Piedmont passed away unexpectedly on November 12, 2025. Rob came into this world with a great zest for life and his enthusiasm was exhibited in all of his endeavors, relationships, and achievements. He was a man of routine and schedules, and believed in being generous, honest, and accountable. His family and community were very strongly impacted by his life force true to his wishes and his loss is felt deeply. He was born in 1952 to veteran parents from the Midwest and grew up in Sacramento next to a creek. From there he ventured to the nearby American River on his bicycle and the Sierra mountains working for the US Forest Service. He was a high academic achiever in his district, took an early interest in engineering, and developed lifelong friendships. Rob graduated from the University of California, Berkeley with bachelor’s and master’s degrees in civil engineering, and a law degree. There he met his fellow law school student and future wife Carola Ingram of Los Angeles, with whom he had three children. He got his pilot’s license and went sky diving, loved the Grateful Dead and photography, and researched earthquakes at the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Center. Working as an attorney in San Francisco in civil engineering and construction cases, Rob found accomplishment in commercial litigation through his understanding of both engineering and legal aspects. He traveled across the country and internationally for work, most recently for the Duane Morris law firm. He said he liked solving problems and helping people solve theirs. He also worked as an arbitrator and was involved in many industry construction forums. A tendency towards identifying right and wrong in law translated to Rob’s interest in sports. He was a coach and referee in his kids’ soccer games, and later switched to rugby as he and his Piedmont resident Rob Hendrickson died on November 12, 2025 sons played the sport. He was a referee or touch judge in most of his younger son’s high school and Cal rugby games. He was a dedicated member of the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) and helped bring on new refs. Rob had a passion for backpacking, skiing, rafting, and scuba diving, often centering vacations around these activities. He loved spending time in Calaveras County, frequently visiting his mountain cabin with his family, friends, and pets. He collected local art and had a personal library of history books about the surrounding areas and the Gold Rush. At home Rob was also interested in gardening, cooking, wine making, reading about geology and evolution (often multiple books at the same time), and the comics. Rob is predeceased by his wife Carola in 2017, and is survived by his sons David and Carl, daughter Katherine, granddaughter Jannah, sister Elisabeth Belle, and brother Lief. Donations to the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) can be made in his honor. A celebration of his life will be held at Piedmont Community Hall.

There he met his fellow law school student and future wife Carola Ingram of Los Angeles, with whom he had three children. He got his pilot’s license and went sky diving, loved the Grateful Dead and photography, and researched earthquakes at the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Center. Working as an attorney in San Francisco in civil engineering and construction cases, Rob found accomplishment in commercial litigation through his understanding of both engineering and legal aspects. He traveled across the country and internationally for work, most recently for the Duane Morris law firm. He said he liked solving problems and helping people solve theirs. He also worked as an arbitrator and was involved in many industry construction forums. A tendency towards identifying right and wrong in law translated to Rob’s interest in sports. He was a coach and referee in his kids’ soccer games, and later switched to rugby as he and his Piedmont resident Rob Hendrickson died on November 12, 2025 sons played the sport. He was a referee or touch judge in most of his younger son’s high school and Cal rugby games. He was a dedicated member of the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) and helped bring on new refs. Rob had a passion for backpacking, skiing, rafting, and scuba diving, often centering vacations around these activities. He loved spending time in Calaveras County, frequently visiting his mountain cabin with his family, friends, and pets. He collected local art and had a personal library of history books about the surrounding areas and the Gold Rush. At home Rob was also interested in gardening, cooking, wine making, reading about geology and evolution (often multiple books at the same time), and the comics. Rob is predeceased by his wife Carola in 2017, and is survived by his sons David and Carl, daughter Katherine, granddaughter Jannah, sister Elisabeth Belle, and brother Lief. Donations to the Northern California Rugby Football Union Referee Society (Pelican Refs) can be made in his honor. A celebration of his life will be held at Piedmont Community Hall.
